content: Many cancer patients experience moderate to severe pain that necessitates treatment with strong opioids. Examples of such opioids include buprenorphine, fentanyl, and morphine. However, not all patients respond effectively to these medications, and some may not tolerate them well. This Cochrane review aimed to evaluate whether buprenorphine provides superior, inferior, or equivalent pain relief and tolerability compared to other analgesic options for cancer-related pain. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and tolerability of buprenorphine in managing cancer pain in both adults and children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, ISI Web of Science, and ISI BIOSIS, up to January 20, 2015. Additional searches were performed in clinical trial registries and conference proceedings. Bibliographic references of identified studies and systematic reviews were also examined, and authors of included studies were contacted for further relevant data. The review included randomized controlled trials with either parallel-group or crossover designs. These trials compared buprenorphine (in any formulation or route of administration) to placebo or other active drugs for managing cancer-related pain. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers using standard Cochrane methodology. Due to the heterogeneity of the data, meta-analysis was not feasible, and the results were summarized narratively. The quality of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE approach. Nineteen studies involving a total of 1,421 patients were included in the review, examining 16 different intervention comparisons. Among the studies comparing buprenorphine to other drugs, 11 conducted comparative analyses between randomized groups. Five studies found buprenorphine to be superior to the comparator, three found no significant differences, and three found buprenorphine to be inferior in terms of side effect profiles or patient acceptability. When comparing different doses or formulations/routes of buprenorphine, one study found no significant differences in pain intensity between intramuscular buprenorphine and buprenorphine suppositories. However, the intramuscular group experienced significantly higher rates of dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and overall adverse events. Sublingual buprenorphine demonstrated a faster onset of pain relief compared to subdermal buprenorphine, with similar durations of analgesia and no significant differences in adverse event rates. For transdermal buprenorphine, two studies found it to be superior to placebo, while a third study found no difference between placebo and various doses of transdermal buprenorphine. Additionally, studies examining different doses of transdermal buprenorphine did not establish a clear dose-response relationship. The quality of the evidence was limited by several factors, including under-reporting of bias assessment items (e.g., patient selection criteria), small sample sizes in many studies, attrition (with missing data for 8.2% of patients for efficacy outcomes and 14.6% for safety outcomes), and incomplete reporting of expected outcomes in some cases. Overall, the evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low quality. In conclusion, the available evidence does not provide a clear understanding of where buprenorphine fits in the treatment of cancer pain compared to other strong opioids. It may be considered a fourth-line option after more standard therapies such as morphine, oxycodone, and fentanyl, and even then, it may only be suitable for select patients. However, the heterogeneity and complexity of palliative care patients highlight the importance of having multiple analgesic options available. Sublingual and injectable buprenorphine appeared to have more consistent analgesic effects, while the transdermal route raised more questions and uncertainties.
